newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Clash looms if Swiss find only few Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Clash looms if Swiss find only few Holocaust funds.

text.p: Swiss bankers and Jewish groups searching for Holocaust victims' unclaimed wealth in Switzerland could be heading for a showdown if -- as many bankers expect -- the latest hunt for lost riches turns up only paltry sums.

Several Swiss bankers say privately that they believe Switzerland was not the big magnet for Jewish wealth before World War Two that groups like the World Jewish Congress (WJC) have made it out to be.

Much of the money that made it here has already been quietly withdrawn by victims' relatives unwilling to share it with family members, or by friends equipped with power of attorney that gave them control over the funds, they say.

This is at odds with barbed allegations from sceptical Jewish groups and a U.S. senator that Swiss banks may silently hold billions of dollars in wealth left by Hitler's victims and have stonewalled relatives trying to track it down.

As uproar mounts, many bankers see these attacks on Switzerland -- made with persistent regularity -- as part of a campaign orchestrated by jealous rivals to undermine Swiss banks' successful expansion in Europe and the United States.
Some are even waiting for the anonymous people believed to be pulling the strings from behind the scenes to come forward and offer to call off the attacks -- for a price.

"This is not about shedding light on history. This is about money," said a senior Swiss banker. He and others said they feared a frontal attack on Switzerland as a financial centre -- perhaps in the form of a boycott call -- if they did not pay up.
"The question is from whom (such a demand would come) and for how much," the banker said, without elaborating.

Maram Stern, assistant secretary-general of the World Jewish Congress, labelled such thinking "complete bullshit...I don't know how they even get this idea," he told Reuters from telephone from Brussels.

Stern, who said he had dealt full-time with the emotional issue of Holocaust accounts for 18 months, said Jewish leaders had made it clear they were not after money but after the truth in tracking down any lost assets.

"Mr (WJC President Edgar) Bronfman has said it over and over clearly. This is not a question of money. It is purely a question of transparency. We want to know what really happened," Stern said, insisting wartime documents now emerging from archives were driving the search.
"What we want is transparency and this is something Swiss banks do not want to hear."
Swiss bankers argue that it would have been very hard for European Jews scared of Hitler's growing power to transfer their wealth to Switzerland in the 1930s.

Even if Jews decided to hide their wealth abroad, they probably would have favoured Britain or the United States as a safe haven rather than Switzerland which could have been steamrollered by Nazi aggression, they say.
Bankers acknowledge neutral Switzerland's solid banks had a reputation as pillars of discretion, but they add that practical problems kept them out of reach for most would-be depositors.

Any funds placed in Swiss banks should still be there if the accounts were never closed. A bigger problem will be finding funds entrusted to private asset managers, not covered by a 1962 Swiss decree for banks to report dormant assets of Nazi victims.
Peter Hug, a historian who has studied the case, said in a recent newspaper interview that it was apparent how much money owned by Holocaust victims was never reported to authorities.
"But I tend to think that the fantastic sums now being bandied about do not correspond to reality," he said.

Carlo Jagmetti, Switzerland's ambassador to Washington, has dismissed as wildly exaggerated the figure of $20 billion that Holocaust survivors are trying to recover from Swiss banks in a class-action lawsuit filed through U.S. courts.

"What is of course amazing is the figure," Jagmetti told reporters. "But we were used to extraordinary figures in other cases and we'll see what happens. For me, I must say these figures are just really speculative."

Banks' searches of their records this year turned up 38.7 million Swiss francs ($30.77 million) deposited by foreign clients before 1945 and whose owners have not been heard from in the past 10 years. Only some of these may have belonged to Holocaust victims, bankers say.
The head of Switzerland's biggest bank has dismissed as "peanuts" the amount of money involved.
As the search gets under way, a Swiss banking ombudsman is coordinating some 1,000 claims that have been submitted, but the WJC has criticised him for failing to turn up any funds so far.

An independent panel set up in May by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers and chaired by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker is soon set to hire auditors to comb banks' records for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous sweeps.
Its search will take at least a year, Volcker has said.
Parliament is also set to give final approval in December to a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a review of the era.

The renewed debate over Switzerland's wartime role -- including its close commercial ties with Nazi Germany that Swiss officials defend as in line with neutrality -- is raising questions about the past that many Swiss had long ignored.

"We have been a nation of moralists, nostalgically immersed in our myth of "everlasting neutrality' and ready at any time to point our finger at "the Germans', "the Serbs', "the Moslems'," said Zurich's Tages-Anzeiger newspaper.
"Now we are experiencing first-hand what it means when the world -- as the result of a completely routine media uproar -- beats up on "the Swiss'." ($1=1.2574 Swiss Franc)
